look_here_first: Start with WOODY SHRUB + small silver/ash-gray fuzzy leaves (densely matted fine hairs) packed along the branches. Then locate ONE tubular, two-lipped, five-lobed lavender to purple flower emerging from a LEAF AXIL. Count four stamens in two length pairs when flower is accessible. The common name 'Texas sage' is NOT Salvia texana.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Much-branched evergreen or seasonally semi-evergreen woody shrub to about 2.5 m; gray older bark, no spines; natural shrubs often irregular rather than sheared balls.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Small simple entire-margined elliptic to obovate blades, mostly under about 2.5 cm, pale gray from dense soft matted trichomes; foliage often crowded on short shoots and sometimes appears paired though generally described as alternate/clustered; distinguish leaf arrangement on several nodes rather than one tight tuft.

key_traits.label: Leaf hairs
key_traits.text: Dense fine soft woolly hairs (tomentum) give ashy silver color; a hand lens and good macro help distinguish hair surface from waxy/glaucous coating.

key_traits.label: Flowers
key_traits.text: Usually solitary in upper leaf axils; pink-lavender to violet, occasionally white; funnel/bell-shaped tubular corolla, five unequal lobes arranged in two lips, throat may have darker spotting and hairs.

key_traits.label: Reproductive
key_traits.text: Usually four fertile stamens (two longer, two shorter, didynamous); superior two-carpellate ovary, mature fruit a dry many-seeded capsule splitting by two valves. Clear stamen/calyx/fruit views needed in final photo polish.

key_traits.label: Habitat
key_traits.text: Limestone/caliche hillsides and dry brushlands, widespread in South Texas and used ornamentally well outside indigenous stands.
